extracted.intended_audience: JOSS reviewers (peer reviewers for the Journal of Open Source Software)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and review criteria for evaluating software submissions and their companion JOSS papers, including repository practices, documentation, functionality, and required paper sections. Intended to guide volunteer reviewers through acceptance/minor/major revision decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: JOSS paper: authors and affiliations
rubrics_metrics.description: The JOSS paper (the compiled PDF associated with this submission) should only include: A list of the authors of the software and their affiliations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper must list authors and affiliations; this is a required element of the submitted paper.

rubrics_metrics.name: JOSS paper: high-level summary for non-specialists
rubrics_metrics.description: The JOSS paper should include a summary describing the high-level functionality and purpose of the software for a diverse, non-specialist audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This summary should be accessible to non-specialists; avoid low-level API details here.

rubrics_metrics.name: JOSS paper: clear statement of need
rubrics_metrics.description: The JOSS paper should include a clear statement of need that illustrates the purpose of the software.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This statement must explain what problem the software solves and why that problem is important (also reiterated in later required 'Statement of need' section).

rubrics_metrics.name: JOSS paper: comparison to other packages
rubrics_metrics.description: The paper should include a description of how this software compares to other commonly-used packages in this research area.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When related tools exist, authors must provide a clear 'build vs. contribute' justification explaining their unique scholarly contribution and why existing alternatives are insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: JOSS paper: mentions of ongoing research or publications
rubrics_metrics.description: The paper should mention (if applicable) any ongoing research projects using the software or recent scholarly publications enabled by it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such mentions are useful evidence of impact or adoption.

rubrics_metrics.name: JOSS paper: key references including software archive link
rubrics_metrics.description: The paper should include a list of key references including a link to the software archive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide persistent links (e.g., DOI, archive) so the software is citable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paper should not include API documentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Note the paper should not include software documentation such as API (Application Programming Interface) functionality, as this should be outlined in the software documentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep API-level details in repository docs; the paper is a high-level description and justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Software license: OSI-approved license file required
rubrics_metrics.description: There should be an OSI approved license included in the repository. ... Note there should be an actual license file present in the repository not just a reference to the license.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acceptable: plain-text LICENSE or COPYING file with the contents of an OSI approved license. Not acceptable: a phrase such as 'MIT license' in a README file.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope and significance
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers should verify that the software demonstrates clear research impact or credible scholarly significance. The submission should show evidence of meaningful contribution to the research community rather than being a one-off tool for a single analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Signals of research impact or scholarly significance may include: published research citing/using the software; evidence of adoption by other groups; integration into workflows; demonstrated performance improvements or novel capabilities; clear potential for reuse and citation. Reviewers should flag questionable scope to the handling editor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Development timeline (sustained development)
rubrics_metrics.description: The project should show evidence of sustained development over time (preferably months or years) rather than rapid, recent code generation. Look for commit history spanning an extended period, iterative improvements and refinements, evolution of features and capabilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good: commits distributed over 6+ months showing gradual feature development. OK: development spanning 6+ months but with sporadic/bursty activity. Not acceptable: all or most commits concentrated in the last few weeks before submission. If clear failure, flag to handling editor for desk rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open development (public history & engagement)
rubrics_metrics.description: The software should have been developed openly from early stages. For projects with recently created public repositories, there should be at least six months of public development history with: evidence of releases or version tags; public issues and/or pull requests; ideally external engagement from users or contributors outside the core team.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good: repository public from inception with documented releases and community interaction. OK: repository public 6+ months ago with evidence of ongoing development. Not acceptable: repository made public immediately before submission with limited public development history. Private development may be acceptable if authors can demonstrate substantial prior effort and 6+ months public availability and use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collaborative effort (multiple contributors & code review)
rubrics_metrics.description: The commit history should show contributions from multiple developers and evidence of iterative refinement through community feedback: multiple contributors, code review via pull requests, responses to issues and feature requests, evidence of community-driven improvements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good: multiple developers with iterative refinement through issues/PRs. OK: single author but shows other evidence of community engagement. Not acceptable: single author with no evidence of community engagement, external use, or collaborative input. For single-author projects, paper evidence of community use or an author list showing collaborative context may suffice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good open-source practices
rubrics_metrics.description: The project should demonstrate that it is a reusable, non-throwaway research software project that follows good open-source practices: license, documentation, quality assurance (tests/CI), releases (tagged versions), and community pathways (contribution guidelines/support channels).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good: all elements present and well-maintained. OK: core elements present (license, docs, tests, contribution guidelines). Bad/not acceptable: missing critical elements or appears to be a one-time code dump.

rubrics_metrics.name: Documentation: README and statement of need
rubrics_metrics.description: There should be sufficient documentation for the reviewer to understand the core functionality of the software. A high-level overview should be included in a README (or equivalent). There should be a statement of need: what problems software is designed to solve, target audience, and its relation to other work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure README contains clear statement of need and pointers to other docs or examples; lack of clear statement is unacceptable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Installation instructions & dependency management
rubrics_metrics.description: Software dependencies should be clearly documented and their installation handled by an automated procedure. Where possible, software installation should be managed with a package manager. Packaging expectations depend on language (e.g., Python packages should be pip installable; Fortran with Makefile may be sufficient).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good: simple to install and follows distribution conventions. OK: list of dependencies plus script (e.g., Makefile). Bad: dependencies unclear and installation lacks automation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Example usage (real-world examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors should include examples of how to use the software (ideally to solve real-world analysis problems).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples help reviewers verify functionality and usefulness; absence weakens evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: API documentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers should check that the software API is documented to a suitable level.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good: all functions/methods documented including example inputs and outputs. OK: core API functionality documented. Bad/not acceptable: API is undocumented. The degree of required API docs is left to reviewer discretion and experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Community guidelines for contributors/support
rubrics_metrics.description: There should be clear guidelines for third-parties wishing to contribute to the software, report issues, or seek support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect CONTRIBUTING.md, issue templates, and clear support channels. These enable sustainable community involvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functionality verification (install & test)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers are expected to install the software they are reviewing and to verify the core functionality of the software.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If installation or verification is impossible, note this in review; automated tests and example inputs help objective checking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tests and continuous integration
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors are strongly encouraged to include an automated test suite covering the core functionality of their software.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good: automated test suite hooked up to continuous integration (GitHub Actions, Circle CI, etc.). OK: documented manual steps to check expected functionality (e.g., sample input file). Bad/not acceptable: no way for reviewer to objectively assess whether the software works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Required paper section: Statement of need (detailed)
rubrics_metrics.description: The paper must have a clearly labeled 'Statement of need' section that: clearly states what problems the software is designed to solve; identifies who the target audience is; explains the software's relation to other work in the field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good: clear problem statement, well-defined target audience, and context. OK: addresses key elements but could be more specific. Bad: vague about the problem, unclear target audience, or missing context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Required paper section: State of the field (build vs contribute justification)
rubrics_metrics.description: The paper must have a 'State of the field' section where authors describe how their software compares to other commonly-used packages and, when related tools exist, provide a 'build vs. contribute' justification explaining their unique scholarly contribution and why existing alternatives are insufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good: thorough comparison and clear explanation of necessity for new tool. OK: identifies related work and explains key differences. Bad: ignores similar tools or fails to justify why not contributing to existing projects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Required paper section: Software design
rubrics_metrics.description: The paper must include a section explaining the architectural choices made: trade-offs considered, the design/architecture chosen and why, and why these choices matter for the research application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good: thoughtful discussion of design decisions and implications. OK: clear explanation with some rationale. Bad: generic code structure description without explaining design reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Required paper section: Research impact statement
rubrics_metrics.description: The paper must provide evidence of either realized impact (publications using the software, evidence of external use/adoption, integration with other research tools) OR credible near-term significance (benchmarks showing improvements, reproducible research materials).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence should be specific and compelling, not merely aspirational. Good: multiple citations, documented external users, or reproducible strong benchmarks. OK: some evidence beyond authors' group or solid benchmarks. Bad: only statements about potential future use without concrete evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Required paper section: AI usage disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: The paper must include a section that transparently discloses any use of generative AI in software creation or development, documentation writing, or paper authoring. If no AI tools were used, this should be explicitly stated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good: clear, specific disclosure of AI tool usage and verification methods. OK: statement that no AI tools were used or general disclosure. Bad: missing section or vague/evasive language about AI usage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorship appropriateness
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers should check whether the submitting author has made a 'substantial contribution' to the submitted software (as determined by the commit history) and whether the full list of paper authors seems appropriate and complete.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors decide co-authorship, but reviewers should flag obvious omissions or mismatches. Financial contributions alone are not sufficient for authorship per JOSS policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Citing prior similar work (novelty vs replication)
rubrics_metrics.description: Submissions that implement solutions already solved in other software packages are accepted provided they meet other criteria and cite prior similar work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers should point out relevant published work that is not yet cited; lack of citation may be grounds to request revisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer grading outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers are asked to grade submissions in one of three categories: 1) Accept 2) Minor Revisions 3) Major Revisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unlike some journals JOSS does not reject outright submissions requiring major revisions; authors are given time to make necessary modifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proprietary/closed-source language submissions
rubrics_metrics.description: Submissions that rely upon a proprietary/closed source language or development environment are acceptable provided they meet other submission requirements and the reviewer is able to install the software & verify functionality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an open-source or free variant exists, reviewers may encourage authors to consider compatibility with that variant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repository hosting requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Repositories must be hosted at a location that allows outside users to freely open issues and propose code changes, such as GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Submissions will not be accepted if the repository is hosted at a location where accounts must be manually approved (or paid for), regardless of who performs the approval.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy on using AI to generate code (refer to JOSS AI policy)
rubrics_metrics.description: JOSS has a detailed policy describing what is considered appropriate use of AI by authors and reviewers. Reviewers should review these guidelines before starting their review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This page links to the detailed policy; reviewers should ensure compliance and that AI usage is disclosed in the paper as required.
